This is referred to as Murphy's sign @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 63 year old female patient complaints of pain in her right knee. You suspect her to be suffering from osteoarthritis after physical examination. You have advised her for physiotherapy. During followup she complains of pain in her right hip as well after 2 months. What nerve supplies both these joints ?
questions.solution: The pain in her hip joint is a referred pain from the knee joint. Obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, and the pain from one joint can be referred to the other. The root value of obturator nerve is ventral division of ventral primary rami of L2, L3 and LA segments of the spinal cord. Femoral nerve also supplies both these joints. Its root value is dorsal division of ventral primary rami of L2, L3 and L4 segments of the spinal cord. Obturator nerve It arises from ventral divisions of ventral primary rami of L2, L3 and L4 segments of spinal cord; whereas femoral nerve arises from dorsal divisions of ventral primary rami of the same segments. Adductor magnus and pectineus are two hybrid or composite muscles Since femoral and obturator nerves supply both the hip joint and knee joint, pain from one joint may be referred to the other joint. Obturator nerve is seen at the medial border of psoas major muscle, crosses the ala of sacrum to enter the pelvis. It exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen to enter the medial aspect of the thigh. Femoral nerve Dorsal divisions of ventral primary rami of lumbar 2, 3, 4 segments of spinal cord Thicker in size Emerges at the lateral border of psoas major Exits from abdomen by passing deep to the inguinal ligament Gives branches in the abdomen to iliacus and pectineus Supplies muscles of front of thigh of, i.e. quadriceps femoris and sartorius. Gives big cutaneous branches. The tibial nerve provides innervation to the muscles of the lower leg and foot. Specifically: triceps sure (the two headed gastocnemius and soleus), plantaris, Popliteus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus. It also has articular and cutaneous branches. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: In Traumatic brain injury, which changes in brain metabolism are seen?

options.label: A
options.text: ↑ CSF Lactate is associated with good Prognosis

questions.solution: In Traumaticbrain injury Anaerobic condition prevails. So brain cells switch to anerobic metabolism producing increasing amount of lactate Now if this lactate is getting utilized as energy source within brain cells through TCA it is associated with good prognosis (means tissue is recovering from injury), However, if the lactate is not getting utilized in brain cells and it will be exported out from cell in to CSF. This outcome means severe damage to brain cells so that they are not able to utilize lactate. Hence increased lactate levels in CSF are associated with poor prognosis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity is decreased due to hypoxic conditions. Now if this lactate is getting utilized as energy source within brain cells through TCA it is associated with good prognosis (means tissue is recovering from injury). However, if the lactate is not getting utilized in brain cells and it will be exported out from cell in to CSF. This outcome means severe damage to brain cells so that they are not able to utilize lactate. Hence increased lactate levels in CSF are associated with poor prognosis. Also, increase lactate uptake from the circulation into brain cells is seen as the injured brain uses lactate as fuel. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Anaerobic condition prevails. So brain cells switch to anerobic metabolism producing increasing amount of lactate
  • Now if this lactate is getting utilized as energy source within brain cells through TCA it is associated with good prognosis (means tissue is recovering from injury),
  • However, if the lactate is not getting utilized in brain cells and it will be exported out from cell in to CSF. This outcome means severe damage to brain cells so that they are not able to utilize lactate. Hence increased lactate levels in CSF are associated with poor prognosis.
  • Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity is decreased due to hypoxic conditions.

questions.stem: A 27 year old had a meal at 9 pm and records blood glucose at 6 am on the next day which was 182 mg/dL. What is the source of glucose in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 27 year old had a meal at 9 pm and records blood glucose at 6 am on the next day which was 182 mg/dL. What is the source of glucose in this patient?
questions.solution: The person is fasting for last 11 hours For upto 2 hours after meals, the source of blood glucose is dietary (food) glucose For next 12-18 hours of fasting, liver glycogenolysis will start and is able to maintain blood glucose Hepatic gluconeogenesis will start only after liver glucogen is exhausted (ie) only after 12 hours onwards The end product of muscle glycogenolysis is glucose 6 phosphate, so muscle glycogen cannot maintain the blood glucose. This is due to the absence of enzyme glucose 6-phosphatase in muscle The Enzyme is only present in liver cells ER and is used to convert glucose 6-phosphate to free glucose @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• The person is fasting for last 11 hours
  • For upto 2 hours after meals, the source of blood glucose is dietary (food) glucose
  • For next 12-18 hours of fasting, liver glycogenolysis will start and is able to maintain blood glucose
  • Hepatic gluconeogenesis will start only after liver glucogen is exhausted (ie) only after 12 hours onwards
  • The end product of muscle glycogenolysis is glucose 6 phosphate, so muscle glycogen cannot maintain the blood glucose. This is due to the absence of enzyme glucose 6-phosphatase in muscle
  • The Enzyme is only present in liver cells ER and is used to convert glucose 6-phosphate to free glucose

questions.stem: Cardiac pain is ischemic pain caused by incomplete obstruction of coronary artery. During myocardial infarction due to ischemia people experience pain on the chest and upper left arm. This pain or angina pectoris is which type of pain?
questions.stemHtml: Cardiac pain is ischemic pain caused by incomplete obstruction of coronary artery. During myocardial infarction due to ischemia people experience pain on the chest and upper left arm. This pain or angina pectoris is which type of pain?
questions.solution: Referred pain is a pain perceived at a location other than the site of painful stimulus/origin. It is the result of a network of a network of interconnecting sensory nerves, that supplies many different tissues. The cardiac pain is an ischemic pain caused by incomplete obstruction of a coronary artery. Axons of pain fibers conveyed by sensory sympathetic cardiac nerves reach T1 - T5 segment of spinal cord mostly through dorsal root of ganglion of left side. Since these DRG also receives sensory impulses from medical side of forearm and upper part of front of chest, pain gets referred to these areas. Radicular pain is a type of pain that radiates from your back and hip into legs through the spine. The pain travels along the spinal nerve root. This occurs when spinal nerve gets compressed or inflamed. Neuropathic pain is a pain condition that is usually chronic, caused by chronic progressive nerve disease and can also occur as the result of injury or infection. It is spontaneous, shooting or burning or electric shock like in character. Somatic pain occurs when pain receptors in tissues (skin, muscle, skeleton, joints, connective tissues) are activated. This type of pain is often described as cramping. Stimuli such as force, temperature, vibration or swelling activate these receptors. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Referred pain is a pain perceived at a location other than the site of painful stimulus/origin. It is the result of a network of a network of interconnecting sensory nerves, that supplies many different tissues.

The cardiac pain is an ischemic pain caused by incomplete obstruction of a coronary artery.

Axons of pain fibers conveyed by sensory sympathetic cardiac nerves reach T1 - T5 segment of spinal cord mostly through dorsal root of ganglion of left side. Since these DRG also receives sensory impulses from medical side of forearm and upper part of front of chest, pain gets referred to these areas.

Radicular pain is a type of pain that radiates from your back and hip into legs through the spine. The pain travels along the spinal nerve root. This occurs when spinal nerve gets compressed or inflamed.

Neuropathic pain is a pain condition that is usually chronic, caused by chronic progressive nerve disease and can also occur as the result of injury or infection. It is spontaneous, shooting or burning or electric shock like in character.

Somatic pain occurs when pain receptors in tissues (skin, muscle, skeleton, joints, connective tissues) are activated. This type of pain is often described as cramping. Stimuli such as force, temperature, vibration or swelling activate these receptors.

Pleura consists of two layers, visceral and parietal; the former is insensitive to pain and the latter is sensitive to pain. The costal part of parietal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves and the mediastinal and central parts of diaphragmatic pleurae are supplied by phrenic (C4) nerve. questions.solution: HEPATIC SEGMENTS On the basis of the intrahepatic distribution of the hepatic artery, the portal vein and the biliary ducts, the liver can be divided into the right and left functionallobes. These do not correspond to the anatomical lobes of the liver. The physiological lobes are separated by a plane passing on the anterosuperior surface along a line joining the cystic notch to the groove for the inferior vena cava. On the inferior surface the plane passes through the fossa for the gallbladder and on the posterior surface it passes through the middle of the caudate lobe The right lobe is subdivided into anterior and posterior segments, and the left lobe into medial and lateral segments. Thus there are four segment in the liver Right anterior (V and VIII), Right posterior (VI and VII), Left lateral (I and III) and Left medial (I and IV). The hepatic segments are of surgical importance. The hepatic veins tend to be intersegmental in their course @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
HEPATIC SEGMENTS

On the basis of the intrahepatic distribution of the hepatic artery, the portal vein and the biliary ducts, the liver can be divided into the right and left functionallobes.

These do not correspond to the anatomical lobes of the liver. The physiological lobes are separated by a plane passing on the anterosuperior surface along a line joining the cystic notch to the groove for the inferior vena cava. On the inferior surface the plane passes through the fossa for the gallbladder and on the posterior surface it passes through the middle of the caudate lobe The right lobe is subdivided into anterior and posterior segments, and the left lobe into medial and lateral segments.

Thus there are four segment in the liver

  1. Right anterior (V and VIII),
  2. Right posterior (VI and VII),
  3. Left lateral (I and III) and
  4. Left medial (I and IV).

The hepatic segments are of surgical importance. The hepatic veins tend to be intersegmental in their course

  • Heat-stable toxin (ST) increases cellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels, whereas heat-labile toxin (LT) causes elevated cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
  • Corynebacterium diphtheria produces toxin that inhibits elongation factor-2 and inhibits protein synthesis.
  • Vibrio cholerae endotoxin increases cAMP and is identical to the heat labile toxin of ETEC.
  • Clostridium difficile exotoxin A and B work by inhibiting protein synthesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about bacterial spore are correct? i) Genus Bacillus and Genus Clostridium form spores in adverse conditions. ii) The spore forms inside the cell and comprise of part of bacterial DNA, and small amount of cytoplasm surrounded by a thick, keratin like coat. iii) Once formed, the spores have no metabolic activity. iv) Formation of spores is also a means of reproduction. v) Spores cannot be killed by boiling; autoclaving at 121°C, usually for 30 minutes, is required. to ensure sterilization.
questions.stemHtml:
Which of the following statements about bacterial spore are correct?
i) Genus Bacillus and Genus Clostridium form spores in adverse conditions.
ii) The spore forms inside the cell and comprise of part of bacterial DNA, and small amount of cytoplasm surrounded by a thick, keratin like coat.
iii) Once formed, the spores have no metabolic activity.
iv) Formation of spores is also a means of reproduction.
v) Spores cannot be killed by boiling; autoclaving at 121°C, usually for 30 minutes, is required. to ensure sterilization.
questions.solution: Spores are highly resistant resting stage formed in unfavorable environmental conditions with low nutrient resources. The spore forms inside the cell and thus is called endospore. It contains the entire bacterial DNA, a small amount of cytoplasm, peptidoglycan, cell membrane and very little water, and most importantly, a thick, keratin like coat that is responsible for the remarkable resistance of the spore to heat, dehydration, radiation, and chemicals. Core contains dipicolinic acid (responsible for heat resistance). Once formed, the spore has no metabolic activity and can remain dormant for many years. Upon exposure to nutrient rich environment, spores germinate into a vegetative cell. Sporulation is not a means of reproduction as one spore gives rise to single vegetative cell. Spores are highly resistant to heat. Therefore, sterilization cannot be achieved by boiling. However, spores of all medically important bacteria are destroyed by autoclaving at 121° C for 15 minutes. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Spores are highly resistant resting stage formed in unfavorable environmental conditions with low nutrient resources.
  • The spore forms inside the cell and thus is called endospore. It contains the entire bacterial DNA, a small amount of cytoplasm, peptidoglycan, cell membrane and very little water, and most importantly, a thick, keratin like coat that is responsible for the remarkable resistance of the spore to heat, dehydration, radiation, and chemicals.
  • Core contains dipicolinic acid (responsible for heat resistance).
  • Once formed, the spore has no metabolic activity and can remain dormant for many years. Upon exposure to nutrient rich environment, spores germinate into a vegetative cell.
  • Sporulation is not a means of reproduction as one spore gives rise to single vegetative cell.
  • Spores are highly resistant to heat. Therefore, sterilization cannot be achieved by boiling. However, spores of all medically important bacteria are destroyed by autoclaving at 121° C for 15 minutes.

questions.solution: Buerger’s disease or thromboangitis obliterans is encountered in heavy smokers, often before the age of 35 years. It begins with nodular phlebitis, followed by raynaud- like cold sensitivity and leg claudication. The vascular insufficiency can lead to excrutating resting pain and ultimately lead to gangrene requiring amputation (b) Behcet’s disease is a neutrophil rich small vessel vasculitis. It presents with recurrent oral ulcers ,anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum and recurrent genital ulcers. It is associated with HLAB51 gene and is positive for pathergy test (c) Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium to large arteries. Also known as pulseless disease due to markedly diminished upper extremity pulses. This disease results in ocular, neurological deficits (d) Kawasaki disease is seen in young children <10 years of age, presents with febrile illness of >5 days, along with polymorphous rashes, cervical lymph node enlargement >1.5 cm, lip swelling, oral congestion, conjunctival congestion, angular chelitis, edema of distal extremities with desquamation of skin @Neet_pg_bot

• Buerger’s disease or thromboangitis obliterans is encountered in heavy smokers, often before the age of 35 years. It begins with nodular phlebitis, followed by raynaud- like cold sensitivity and leg claudication. The vascular insufficiency can lead to excrutating resting pain and ultimately lead to gangrene requiring amputation

(b) Behcet’s disease is a neutrophil rich small vessel vasculitis. It presents with recurrent oral ulcers ,anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum and recurrent genital ulcers. It is associated with HLAB51 gene and is positive for pathergy test

(c) Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium to large arteries. Also known as pulseless disease due to markedly diminished upper extremity pulses. This disease results in ocular, neurological deficits

questions.solution: The genital ulcers shown in the image point to HSV 2 infection. HSV-2 is found latent in the sacral ganglia. Reactivation of HSV-2 genital infection can occurs frequently, and may be asymptomatic. Even in asymptomatic HSV2 infection, viral shedding can occur resulting in transmission of virus through genital secretions. When symptomatic, local symptoms such as pain and itching, and systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, and myalgias are present. questions.solution: SAFE strategy developed by the WHO is the key to the treatment of trachoma. This consists of Surgery on the lids. Antibiotics to treat the community pool of infection, Facial cleanliness (SAFE) and Environmental changes Blindness from Trachoma can be stop at four Blindness From Trachoma can be stop at four different points : SAFE S - Surgical correction for trichiasis. It is a simple operation that can turn out lashes which are scratching the cornea. patients can be operated on in a local dispensary or health center, or other community space if properly prepared. The surgical procedure can be performed by those who have had surgical training : eye doctors, eye nurses or eye care assistants. A - Antibiotic treatment of people with active trachoma infection.Regular detection and treatment of people with active trachoma is important. The recommended treatment is as follows : Wash the face and clean the eyes Apply tetracycline 1% ointment to both eyes two times daily for six weeks The ointment is sticky and may blur the vision for a few moments. This will only last a few moments. If possible, treat all the children in the family. F - Clean Faces Families and individuals can do something to protect themselves from infection by increasing the number of times a child washes Apply tetracycline Ivo ointment to Dom eyes two times daily for six weeks The ointment is sticky and may blur the vision for a few moments. This will only last a few moments. If possible, treat all the children in the family. F - Clean Faces Families and individuals can do something to protect themselves from infection by increasing the number of times a child washes his/her face. Regular face washing removes discharge so that flies are not attracted to faces. It does not require great quantities of water: one liter of water can wash up to 30 faces. E - Environmental Improvement It is a global initiative to eliminate trachoma as a blinding disease, entitled GET 2020 (Global Elimination of Trachoma), was launched under WHO's leadership in 1997. @Neet_pg_bot

Antibiotics to treat the community pool of infection, Facial cleanliness (SAFE) and Environmental changes Blindness from Trachoma can be stop at four Blindness From Trachoma can be stop at four different points : SAFE

S - Surgical correction for trichiasis. It is a simple operation that can turn out lashes which are scratching the cornea. patients can be operated on in a local dispensary or health center, or other community space if properly prepared. The surgical procedure can be performed by those who have had surgical training : eye doctors, eye nurses or eye care assistants.

A - Antibiotic treatment of people with active trachoma infection.Regular detection and treatment of people with active trachoma is important. The recommended treatment is as follows :

  • Wash the face and clean the eyes
  • Apply tetracycline 1% ointment to both eyes two times daily for six weeks
  • The ointment is sticky and may blur the vision for a few moments. This will only last a few moments. If possible, treat all the children in the family.

F - Clean Faces

Families and individuals can do something to protect themselves from infection by increasing the number of times a child washes Apply tetracycline Ivo ointment to Dom eyes two times daily for six weeks

  • The ointment is sticky and may blur the vision for a few moments. This will only last a few moments. If possible, treat all the children in the family.

F - Clean Faces

Families and individuals can do something to protect themselves from infection by increasing the number of times a child washes his/her face. Regular face washing removes discharge so that flies are not attracted to faces. It does not require great quantities of water: one liter of water can wash up to 30 faces.

E - Environmental Improvement

It is a global initiative to eliminate trachoma as a blinding disease, entitled GET 2020 (Global Elimination of Trachoma), was launched under WHO's leadership in 1997.

Lets first see what skewed distribution curve is. An asymmetrical distribution curve can be of two types: 1. Positive skewed distribution curve 2. Negative skewed distribution curve Positive (or right) and negative (or left) skewed curves are recognized by the location of the tail of the curve (not by the location of the hump - a common error) Positive or Right skewed distribution curve there curves have a relatively large number of low scores and a small no of very high scores the mean lies towards the extreme right of the curve Negative or left skewed distribution curve. there curves have a large number of high scores and a relatively small number of low scores the mean lies towards the extreme left of the curve. Now lets see the measures of central tendency. Mode is the most frequently occurring value it lies at the peak of the hump. Mean is the arithmetic average it is greatly influenced by the relatively small number of very high or very low scores it lies towards the extreme right in a right (Positive) distribution curve and towards the extreme left in a left (negative) distribution curve. Median is the middle value it lies b/w the mean and mode dividing the curve into two equal halves. Relationship b/w the measures of central tendency In a symmetrical curve Mean = Median = Mode In a Positive (Right) skewed curve Mean > Median > Mode In a Negative (left) skewed curve Mean < Median < Mode @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation is used to visualize fungus in a sample. KOH works by dissolving the host cells and bacteria and spares fungi. Cryptococcus neoformans in cerebrospinal fluid is visualized by India Ink preparation. These yeast cells are identified by large transparent capsules that exclude the India ink particles. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen stain (the classic acid-fast stain). ZN staining is used to identify organisms with mycolic acid in their walls. Mycolic acid in the walls makes the bacterium acid fast and thus they can resist decolorization due to acidic alcohol. Most bacteria with crystal violet and iodine are stained purple in color. Upon treating the stained cells with acetone, gram-positive organisms can retain stain, whereas gram-negative species, such as Escherichia coli, lose the stain, becoming colorless. Counterstaining with safranin is needed to visualize E.coli which stains gram-negative bacteria pink or red. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which process of DNA transfer uses a bacteriophage to convert non-toxin producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae to toxin producing strains?
questions.stemHtml: Which process of DNA transfer uses a bacteriophage to convert non-toxin producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae to toxin producing strains?
questions.solution: Transduction refers to DNA transfer by means of a bacterial virus (bacteriophage). It is of two types- a) Generalised and b) Specialised In generalized type, the lytic phage infects the bacterium and breaks down the bacterial DNA. During packaging of virus particles, the bacterial DNA can accidently become part of the viral capsid. This bacteriophage then infects another bacterium, thus transferring the bacterial genes. In specialized type of transduction, the bacteriophage (lysogenic phage) incorporates into bacterial DNA. When phage DNA is excised, flanking bacterial genes may be excised with it. DNA is packaged into phage capsid and can infect another bacterium. Lysogenic phage helps in incorporating toxins producing genes in non-toxin producing strains like Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Clostridium botulinum, Group A streptococci. @Neet_pg_bot

(a) Giant cell arteritis is characterized by focal granulomatous inflammation of medium and small arteries, chiefly cranial vessels and most commonly temporal arteries in elderly people. Visual disturbance, polymyalgia rheumatica and flu like symptoms are also seen

(c) polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic disease characterized by necrotising inflammation throughout the wall of various small to medium sized arteries. This is associated with hematuria, albuminuria ,hypertension, diffuse myalgia and peripheral neuritis. Sometimes maybe associated with hepatitis b antigen and deposited immune complexes are the pathogenetic feature

(d) Hyaline arteriosclerosis is typically seen in elderly patients particularly those with mild hypertension and diabetis mellitus. Microscopically there is diffuse, pink ,hyaline thickening of arteriole walls, this is a major microscopic feature of benign nephrosclerosis

questions.solution: Zenker’s diverticulum MC type of esophageal diverticulum It is a false diverticulum (mucosa & submucosa) MC in elderly / diabetic / males Inferior constrictor muscle has dual nerve supply Thyropharyngeus – supplied by pharyngeal plexus Cricopharyngeus – supplied by RLN Due to this dual nerve supply – neuromuscular incoordination during swallowing leads to herniation through killian’s dehiscence due to increased pressure Symptoms MC symptom – dysphagia >50% of cases – Zenker’s diverticula is associated with cervical web. Halitosis Regurgitation Complications Increased risk of aspiration (due to regurgitation) ↓ Increased of pneumonitis ↓ Increased risk of lung abscess (MC complication lung abscess) Increased risk of SCC (due to chronic inflammation at Zenker’s diverticula) Investigation IOC for Dx – Barium swallow Treatment Treatment of choice – cricopharyngealmyotomy + diverticulopexy Other alternative procedures Diverticulectomy (for larger diverticula’s >4 cm) Dohlman procedure Dohlman’s procedure Aka diverticula-esophagostomy It is endoscopic stapling of septum located between esophagus & diverticula @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Zenker’s diverticulum

  • MC type of esophageal diverticulum
  • It is a false diverticulum (mucosa & submucosa)
  • MC in elderly / diabetic / males
  • Inferior constrictor muscle has dual nerve supply
    • Thyropharyngeus – supplied by pharyngeal plexus
    • Cricopharyngeus – supplied by RLN
    • Due to this dual nerve supply – neuromuscular incoordination during swallowing leads to herniation through killian’s dehiscence due to increased pressure

Symptoms

  • MC symptom – dysphagia
  • >50% of cases – Zenker’s diverticula is associated with cervical web.
  • Halitosis
  • Regurgitation

Complications

  • Increased risk of aspiration (due to regurgitation)

↓

Increased of pneumonitis

↓

Increased risk of lung abscess (MC complication lung abscess)

  • Increased risk of SCC (due to chronic inflammation at Zenker’s diverticula)

Investigation

  • IOC for Dx – Barium swallow

Treatment

  • Treatment of choice – cricopharyngealmyotomy + diverticulopexy
  • Other alternative procedures
    • Diverticulectomy (for larger diverticula’s >4 cm)
    • Dohlman procedure

Dohlman’s procedure

  • Aka diverticula-esophagostomy
  • It is endoscopic stapling of septum located between esophagus & diverticula

questions.solution: Postoperative endophthalmitis is a serious complication that can happen after cataract surgery. It occurs mainly due to invasion of the globe by microbial flora, bacteria, or fungi from the adnexa and environment during the time of surgery. The features described is diagnostic of left sided tension pneumothorax

Tension Pneumothorax

Presentation

  • Acute respiratory distress
  • Hypotension
  • Raised jugular venous pressure
  • Tracheal deviation away from the pneumothorax side
  • Reduced air entry on affected side

Management of a tension pneumothorax

If strong clinical suspicion, give high-flow oxygen and insert large-bore cannula into second intercostal space in midclavicular line on side of pneumothorax

  • Do not wait for a chest X-ray if patient seriously compromised or cardiac arrest has occurred or if the diagnosis is clinically certain
  • Hiss of escaping air confirms diagnosis
  • Air should be aspirated until the patient is less distressed. Then interest a chest drain in mid-axillary line, leaving the cannula in place until you have finished and the underwater seal is bubbling satisfactorily

Comparing simple and tension pneumothorax

Simple pneumothorax Tension Pneumothorax
Trachea ↓ Trachea →
Expansion ↓ Expansion ↓
Precussion Note ↑ Precussion Note ↑
Breathe sounds → Breathe sounds →
Neck Veins ↑

PNEUMOTHORAX TYPES

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax

  • Occurs without an apparent cause

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax

  • Occurs in presence of existing lung pathology e,g, COPD

Simple pneumothorax

  • Non-expanding collection of air around the lung

Tension pneumothorax

  • Expanding collection of air around the lung

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about auditory ossicles is NOT true?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about auditory ossicles is NOT true?

options.label: A
options.text: Malleus and incus develop mainly from the first brachial arch

options.label: B
options.text: The foot plate of the stapes is held in the oval window by annular ligament

options.label: C
options.text: The incudostapedial joint is an example of a ball and socket joint

options.label: D
options.text: The head of the malleus is embedded in the fibrous layer of tympanic membrane

questions.answerText: The head of the malleus is embedded in the fibrous layer of tympanic membrane
questions.solution: There are three ossicles in the middle ear-the malleus, incus and stapes. The malleus has head, neck, handle (manubrium), a lateral and an anterior process. The head and neck of malleus are present in the attic while the manubrium of malleus is embedded in the fibrous layer of the tympanic membrane. The lateral process forms a knob like projection on the outer surface of the tympanic membrane and gives attachment to the anterior and posterior malleal (malleolar) folds. The incus has a body and a short process, both of which lie in the attic, and a long process which hangs vertically and attaches to the head of stapes. The stapes has a head, neck, anterior and posterior crura, and a footplate. The footplate is held in the oval window by annular ligament. There are two joints between the ossicles- incudomalleolar and incudostapedial joint. The incudomalleolar is a saddle joint whereas the incudostapedial joint is an example of a ball and socket joint. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• There are three ossicles in the middle ear-the malleus, incus and stapes.
  • The malleus has head, neck, handle (manubrium), a lateral and an anterior process. The head and neck of malleus are present in the attic while the manubrium of malleus is embedded in the fibrous layer of the tympanic membrane. The lateral process forms a knob
  • like projection on the outer surface of the tympanic membrane and gives attachment to the anterior and posterior malleal (malleolar) folds.
  • The incus has a body and a short process, both of which lie in the attic, and a long process which hangs vertically and attaches to the head of stapes.
  • The stapes has a head, neck, anterior and posterior crura, and a footplate. The footplate is held in the oval window by annular ligament.
  • There are two joints between the ossicles- incudomalleolar and incudostapedial joint. The incudomalleolar is a saddle joint whereas the incudostapedial joint is an example of a ball and socket joint.

questions.solution: VELAMENTOUS PLACENTA and Vasa Previa VELAMENTOUS PLACENTA -The cord is attached to the membranes. The branching vessels traverse between the membranes for a varying distance before they reach and supply the placenta. If the leash of blood vessels happen to traverse through the membranes overlying the internal os, in front of the presenting part, the condition is called vasa previa. questions.stemHtml: In a patient, Rinne test positive in both ears, Weber's lateralizes to the right. This implies:
questions.solution: Interpretation of the Rinne test is as following- Normally, AC is 2 times better than BC (+ve Rinne). Conductive deafness, AC lesser than BC (–ve Rinne). Sensorineural (SN) deafness, AC greater than BC [but, duration is reduced] (low +ve Rinne). For Weber’s test In conductive deafness, the sound is lateralized to deaf ear and in bilateral conductive loss to the deafer ear or it is centrally heard if both ears are equally deaf. It is because ambient noise does not disturb the diseased ear as much as the normal ear. In sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), sound is lateralized to better hearing ear or is heard centrally if both ears are equally bad. In normal ear, no lateralization of sound occurs. For this patient, Rinne test positive in both ears indicates either hearing is normal or there is SNHL. Weber lateralizes to the right means that the left ear has SNHL. This cannot be conductive hearing loss of any side as Rinne is positive. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Interpretation of the Rinne test is as following-

  • Normally, AC is 2 times better than BC (+ve Rinne).
  • Conductive deafness, AC lesser than BC (–ve Rinne).
  • Sensorineural (SN) deafness, AC greater than BC [but, duration is reduced] (low +ve Rinne).

For Weber’s test

  • In conductive deafness, the sound is lateralized to deaf ear and in bilateral conductive loss to the deafer ear or it is centrally heard if both ears are equally deaf. It is because ambient noise does not disturb the diseased ear as much as the normal ear.
  • In sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), sound is lateralized to better hearing ear or is heard centrally if both ears are equally bad.
  • In normal ear, no lateralization of sound occurs.

For this patient, Rinne test positive in both ears indicates either hearing is normal or there is SNHL. Weber lateralizes to the right means that the left ear has SNHL. This cannot be conductive hearing loss of any side as Rinne is positive.

questions.stemHtml: A 36 year old female presents to the hospital with abdominal pain. She is also taking medications for her gout. USG reveals stone in her kidney. What is the most common type of stone formed in gout patients:
questions.solution: Types of Renal Stones Ca Oxalate stones Most common type of renal stones Radiopaque Risk factors Hypercalcemia Hypercalciuria Hyperoxaluria Uric acid stones Most common type of radiolucent renal stone Risk factors Cout Lesch- Nyhan syndrome Myeloproliferative disorders (due to increased breakdown of cells) (Hypoxanthine Xanthine →Uric Acid) Management Principles If acidic stone - do alkalinisation of urine If basic stone - do acidification of urine. Acid combines with base & forms salt which is soluble is excreted in urine. Plenty of fluids Low purine diet Acetazolamideis used for Alkalinisation of urine Allopurinol - To block conversion of Hypoxanthine to xanthine & hence block formation of uric acid. Struvite stones Aka staghorn calculi / Triple phosphate stone (Ca, Mg, Nh4+, Phosphate) MC in females because of short urethra (4cm) Short urethra – Increased risk of UTI → Proteus → produces urease Urease converts urea into ammonia – Ammonia gets precipitated 3-5 minor calyces join major calyx and later forms pelvis, pelvic ureteric junction and then ureter Struvite stone is very large & fills pelvic calyceal system and looks like staghorn (due to branching in stone) → very large silent destruction of kidney Management Sandwich Technique – PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) + ESWL (Extra corporeal shock wave lithotripsy) To prevent recurrence of stone formation – Irreversible inhibitor of urease (AcetoxyHydroxamic acid ) Cystine stones Seen in cystinuria Radio Opaque (double sulphide bond) Very Hard (not easily broken by ESWL) Crystal – Benzene shaped Crystal (Hexagonal Crystal) D – Penicillamine a-MPG (Alpha-mercaptopropionyl glycine) (Alpha MPG>D -penicillamine) Alpha – MPG – Better tolerated Xanthine stones Seen in xanthinuria Hypoxanthine – xanthine (Allopurinol can be used to block conversion of Hypoxanthine to xanthine) Radiolucent Brick-red in color Lamination on cross section @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Types of Renal Stones

Ca Oxalate stones

  • Most common type of renal stones
  • Radiopaque
  • Risk factors
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypercalciuria
  • Hyperoxaluria

Uric acid stones

  • Most common type of radiolucent renal stone

Risk factors

  • Cout
  • Lesch- Nyhan syndrome
  • Myeloproliferative disorders (due to increased breakdown of cells)
  • (Hypoxanthine Xanthine →Uric Acid)

Management Principles

If acidic stone - do alkalinisation of urine

  • If basic stone - do acidification of urine.
  • Acid combines with base & forms salt which is soluble is excreted in urine.
  • Plenty of fluids
  • Low purine diet
  • Acetazolamideis used for Alkalinisation of urine
  • Allopurinol - To block conversion of Hypoxanthine to xanthine & hence block formation of uric acid.

Struvite stones

  • Aka staghorn calculi / Triple phosphate stone (Ca, Mg, Nh4+, Phosphate)
  • MC in females because of short urethra (4cm)
  • Short urethra – Increased risk of UTI → Proteus → produces urease
  • Urease converts urea into ammonia – Ammonia gets precipitated
  • 3-5 minor calyces join major calyx and later forms pelvis, pelvic ureteric junction and then ureter
  • Struvite stone is very large & fills pelvic calyceal system and looks like staghorn (due to branching in stone) → very large silent destruction of kidney

Management

  • Sandwich Technique – PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) + ESWL (Extra corporeal shock wave lithotripsy)
  • To prevent recurrence of stone formation – Irreversible inhibitor of urease (AcetoxyHydroxamic acid )

Cystine stones

  • Seen in cystinuria
  • Radio Opaque (double sulphide bond)
  • Very Hard (not easily broken by ESWL)
  • Crystal – Benzene shaped Crystal (Hexagonal Crystal)
  • D – Penicillamine
  • a-MPG (Alpha-mercaptopropionyl glycine) (Alpha MPG>D -penicillamine) Alpha – MPG – Better tolerated

Xanthine stones

  • Seen in xanthinuria
  • Hypoxanthine – xanthine (Allopurinol can be used to block conversion of Hypoxanthine to xanthine)
  • Radiolucent
  • Brick-red in color
  • Lamination on cross section

questions.solution: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) Caused by increased secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) from abnormal parathyroid gland More common in females MC cause of PHPT – solitary adenoma (80% of cases) MC location – inferior parathyroid Increased PTH leads to hypercalcemia Mechanism that can leads to hypercalcemia Increased GI absorption of calcium Decreased renal calcium clearance Increased production of vitamin D3 Etiology Familial predisposition Exposure of low therapeutic ionizing radiation Declining renal function with age Alteration in the sensitivity of parathyroid gland to suppression – by calcium Lithium therapy Most cases of PHPT are sporadic It is associated with – MEN-1, MEN 2A, isolated familial HPT, familial HPT with jaw tumor syndrome Clinical features S/P Resorption Radial side Middle phalanx 2nd / 3rd fingers Skull – salt & pepper App. Cystic lesion → haemorrhage → OFC (Osteitis cystica) → Brown Tumor (Hemosiderin) Classical pentad Kidney stone Painful bones Abdominal groans Psychic moans Fatigue over tones Increased concentration of PTH – elevated immunoreactivePTH in asymptomatichypercalcemia Decreased serum phosphate & increased 24 hours urinary calcium Most widely used an accurate investigation for localization of parathyroid adenoma – Tc labelled Sestamibi scan X-ray findings of hands Subperiosteal resorption – most apparent on radial aspect of – middle phalanx of 2nd & 3rd finger Bone cyst Tufting of distal phalanges Management Basic principles of management 1. SERM (selective estrogen receptor modulator) or Bisphosphonates (IV ibandronate) To decrease Ca2+ level To increase bone mineral density 2. Parathyroidectomy if patient has Classical pentad (or) Age <50 years Steps in management of PHTP 1. Correction of hypercalcemia – by IV normal saline followed by forced diuresis with furosemide 2. Neck exploration Single adenoma (80-85% cases) – Resection Two adenomas (5% cases) – Resection Hyperplasia of all 4 glands (10-15% cases) Excision of 3 and half gland or Excision of all 4 glands Note Accidentally removed parathyroid gland during thyroidectomy – should be auto transplanted into belly of sternocleidomastoid muscle, (PTG are broken into 1 mm pieces for placing into SCM) Site of transplantation is marked with suture / clip. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT)

  • Caused by increased secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) from abnormal parathyroid gland
  • More common in females
  • MC cause of PHPT – solitary adenoma (80% of cases)
    • MC location – inferior parathyroid
  • Increased PTH leads to hypercalcemia
  • Mechanism that can leads to hypercalcemia
    • Increased GI absorption of calcium
    • Decreased renal calcium clearance
    • Increased production of vitamin D3

Etiology

  • Familial predisposition
  • Exposure of low therapeutic ionizing radiation
  • Declining renal function with age
  • Alteration in the sensitivity of parathyroid gland to suppression – by calcium
  • Lithium therapy

Most cases of PHPT are sporadic

It is associated with – MEN-1, MEN 2A, isolated familial HPT, familial

HPT with jaw tumor syndrome

Clinical features

S/P Resorption

  • Radial side
  • Middle phalanx
  • 2nd / 3rd fingers

Skull – salt & pepper App.

Cystic lesion → haemorrhage → OFC (Osteitis cystica) → Brown Tumor (Hemosiderin)

  • Classical pentad
    • Kidney stone
    • Painful bones
    • Abdominal groans
    • Psychic moans
    • Fatigue over tones

  • Increased concentration of PTH – elevated immunoreactivePTH in asymptomatichypercalcemia
  • Decreased serum phosphate & increased 24 hours urinary calcium
  • Most widely used an accurate investigation for localization of parathyroid adenoma – Tc labelled Sestamibi scan
  • X-ray findings of hands
    • Subperiosteal resorption – most apparent on radial aspect of – middle phalanx of 2nd & 3rd finger
    • Bone cyst
    • Tufting of distal phalanges

Management

  • Basic principles of management

1. SERM (selective estrogen receptor modulator) or Bisphosphonates (IV ibandronate)

  • To decrease Ca2+ level
  • To increase bone mineral density

2. Parathyroidectomy

  • if patient has
  • Classical pentad (or)
  • Age <50 years

Steps in management of PHTP

1. Correction of hypercalcemia – by IV normal saline followed by forced diuresis with furosemide

2. Neck exploration

  • Single adenoma (80-85% cases) – Resection
  • Two adenomas (5% cases) – Resection
  • Hyperplasia of all 4 glands (10-15% cases)
    • Excision of 3 and half gland or
    • Excision of all 4 glands

Note

  • Accidentally removed parathyroid gland during thyroidectomy – should be auto transplanted into belly of sternocleidomastoid muscle, (PTG are broken into 1 mm pieces for placing into SCM)
  • Site of transplantation is marked with suture / clip.

questions.solution: KERATOSIS OBTURANS is accumulation of desquamated keratin in the external auditory meatus. Also called as canal wall cholesteatoma M/C in young patients. questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old lady with rheumatoid arthritis is experiencing dry eyes. A Schirmer's test reveals reduced tear production, whereas a rose Bengal stain reveals corneal ulcers. What is the ONE MOST LIKELY DISEASE?
questions.solution: Sjogren's syndrome Sjogren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder affecting exocrine glands resulting indr mucosal surfaces. Sjogren syndrome may be seen alone (primary) or in associationwit other autoimmune diseases (secondary) such as rheumatoid arthritis, primarybiliary cirrhosis, or systemic lupus erythematosus. As Sjogren's syndrome progresses, it becomes a systemic disease involving majororgans (lungs, kidneys, etc.) and may eventually evolve into a lymphoproliferativedisease - malignant Lymphoma. Note that sjogren's syndrome is much more common in females (ratio 9:1) Features dry eyes: keratoconjunctivitis sicca Patients complain of itchy eyes, sandy feeling under their eyes (because ofdecreasec lacrimal production) dry mouth Patients may complain of difficulty swallowing food vaginal dryness parotid enlargement Bilateral enlargement of the parotid glands Investigation Schirmer's test will show decreased tear production Rose Bengal stain will document corneal ulcerations ANAs will be positive and specifically anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) rheumatoid factor (RF) positive in nearly of patients Management There is no cure for sjogren’s syndrome. Artificial tears may help with the dry eyes. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Sjogren's syndrome

Sjogren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder affecting exocrine glands resulting indr mucosal surfaces. Sjogren syndrome may be seen alone (primary) or in associationwit other autoimmune diseases (secondary) such as rheumatoid arthritis, primarybiliary cirrhosis, or systemic lupus erythematosus.

As Sjogren's syndrome progresses, it becomes a systemic disease involving majororgans (lungs, kidneys, etc.) and may eventually evolve into a lymphoproliferativedisease - malignant Lymphoma. Note that sjogren's syndrome is much more common in females (ratio 9:1)

Features

dry eyes: keratoconjunctivitis sicca

  • Patients complain of itchy eyes, sandy feeling under their eyes (because ofdecreasec lacrimal production) dry mouth
  • Patients may complain of difficulty swallowing food vaginal dryness parotid enlargement
  • Bilateral enlargement of the parotid glands

Investigation

  • Schirmer's test will show decreased tear production
  • Rose Bengal stain will document corneal ulcerations
  • ANAs will be positive and specifically anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB)
  • rheumatoid factor (RF) positive in nearly of patients

Management

  • There is no cure for sjogren’s syndrome. Artificial tears may help with the dry eyes.

questions.stemHtml: Over the last two days, a 50-year-old guy has developed a red, sensitive, and swollen left foot. He is unable to bear weight due to the severity of the pain. He had a myocardial infarction four weeks ago and is now suffering from heart failure. His cardiologist recently prescribed meds for him. Which of the drugs is most likely to blame for the swelling in his left foot?
questions.solution: This man was likely prescribed furosemide to combat the fluid overload from the heart failure. Furosemide may raise uric acid levels and precipitate gout. Gout most commonly affects the metatarsophalangeal joint of the first toe but question writers will not make questions that obvious and often they may describe it as left foot swelling and pain. Other common precipitants of gout are: Excessive amounts of alcohol Thiazide diuretics like bendroflumethiazide @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
ADPKD [Autosomal Dominant Polysctic Kidney Disease]

  • Invovlvement of chromosome 16, 4
  • Abnomral protein – Polycystin

Clinical Features

  • Usually presented on 3rd to 4th decade
  • MC – Hypertension (75% Adults & 25% Children)
  • Other Presentations
  • Polyuria
  • Nocturia
  • Hematuria
  • Nephrolithiasis
  • MC cause of death – Cardovascular disorders
  • CRF
  • Uusally in 5th to 6th decade

  • Polycystic Liver Disease (MC)
  • Cyst in Ovary, Pancreas, Spleen
  • Mitral Valve prolapses
  • Berry Aneurysm
  • Colonic diverticulosis
  • Arachnoid cyst

  • IOC – CECT

Management

  • ROVSING’S Operation – Deroofing of Cyst in ADPKD
  • ROVSING’s Syndrome – Hyperextension of spiene in proudcues abdominal Pain, Nausea, Vomitting in horse shoe kidney
  • ROVSING Sign – Pain in right iliac fossa on pressing left iliac fossa

questions.stem: Which of the following statement about tympanic membrane is false?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statement about tympanic membrane is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Tympanic membrane is positioned at an angle of 55 degrees to the external auditory canal

options.label: B
options.text: IX cranial nerve’s tympanic branch supplies the medial part of tympanic membrane

options.label: C
options.text: The cone of light forms on anterosuperior quadrant

options.label: D
options.text: Pars tensa forms most of the tympanic membrane and is less mobile than pars flaccida

questions.answerText: The cone of light forms on anterosuperior quadrant
questions.solution: Tympanic membrane forms the partition between the external acoustic canal and the middle ear. It is obliquely set and as a result, its posterosuperior part is more lateral than its anteroinferior part. Tympanic membrane comprises of two parts: Pars Tensa and Pars Flaccida. Pars tensa forms most part of tympanic membrane. A bright cone of light can be seen radiating from the tip of malleus to the periphery in the anteroinferior quadrant. Pars Flaccida (Sharpnell’s Membrane)is present above the lateral process of malleus between the notch of Rivinus and and the anterior and Posterior malleal folds (earlier called malleolar folds). It is not so taut and may appear slightly pinkish. In terms of nerve supply of tympanic membrane, the lateral or outer surface’s anterior half is supplied by auriculotemporal nerve and posterior half by the vagus nerve (Arnold nerve). The medial or inner surface is innervated by Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson’s nerve) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Tympanic membrane forms the partition between the external acoustic canal and the middle ear. It is obliquely set and as a result, its posterosuperior part is more lateral than its anteroinferior part.
  • Tympanic membrane comprises of two parts: Pars Tensa and Pars Flaccida.
  • Pars tensa forms most part of tympanic membrane. A bright cone of light can be seen radiating from the tip of malleus to the periphery in the anteroinferior quadrant.
  • Pars Flaccida (Sharpnell’s Membrane)is present above the lateral process of malleus between the notch of Rivinus and and the anterior and Posterior malleal folds (earlier called malleolar folds). It is not so taut and may appear slightly pinkish.
  • In terms of nerve supply of tympanic membrane, the lateral or outer surface’s anterior half is supplied by auriculotemporal nerve and posterior half by the vagus nerve (Arnold nerve). The medial or inner surface is innervated by Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson’s nerve)

questions.solutionHtml:
This woman has become acutely breathless from a pulmonary emboli. She is hypoxic and, as a reflex to this, is hyperventilating (as evidenced by the low PaCO2). As a result, she has developed an alkalosis.

The other options are much less likely to be the answer:

Diabetic ketoacidosis and methanol overdose → both causes acidosis. The scenario that was given is alkalosis

Panic attacks → This does cause acute alkalosis via hyperventilation (and therefore low PaCO2 and a high pH), but tends to happen in the absence of hypoxia rather than as a response to it (as in pulmonary embolism)

To understand this question, we have to go back to basics.

First, is the patient hypoxic?

  • the Pa02 > 10is normal

Second, is the patient acidaemic (pH<73.35) or alkalaemic (pH>7.45)

Third, what is the respiratory component: What has happened to the PaCO2?

  • PaCO2 > 6.0 kPasuggests a respiratory acidosis (or respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis) PaCO2 < 4.7 kPasuggests a respiratory alkalosis (or respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis)

Fourth, what is the metabolic component: What is the bicarbonate level/base excess?

  • bicarbonate <22 mmol/l suggests a metabolic acidosis (or renal compensation for a respiratory alkalosis)
  • bicarbonate > 26 mmol/l suggests a metabolic alkalosis (or renal compensation for a respiratory acidosis)

In summary

She has developed respiratory alkalosis with very minimal renal compensation taking into account that renal compensation usually takes around 48 hours to manifest.

ARTERIAL BLOOD GASES, CASUES

METABOLIC ACIDIOSIS

  • Excess Production of Organic Acids
  • Ketoacidosis
  • Alcoholic
  • Violent convulsions
  • Excessive ingestion of Toxins
  • Aspirin
  • Methanol Alcohol
  • Excess loss of HCO3
  • Diarrhoea
  • Addison’s disease
  • Retention of Organic Acids
  • Renal insufficiency of Any Cause

METABOLIC ALKALOSIS

  • HCI loss
  • Vomiting
  • Excessive Administration of HCO3
  • Hypovolaemia
  • Increased Renal Excretion of Acid
  • Diuretic therapy
  • Secondary Hypoparathyroidism
RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS
  • Airway obstruction
  • Aspiration
  • COPD
  • Respiratory center depression
  • Circulatory collapse
  • Cardiac arrest
  • Pulmonary oedema
  • Neurogenic causes
  • Cervical spine injury
  • Drugs (paralytic agents, organophosphates)
  • Restrictive effects
  • Haemothorax
  • Pneumothorax

questions.stemHtml:
Muscle weakness is present in a 60-year-old male. He has trouble walking for lengthy periods of time or climbing stairs. It's difficult to do things like stand up from a seated posture. He also has trouble swallowing some foods. His blood tests reveal the following:
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 149 U/L
Aspartatetransaminase (AST) 37 U/L
Alaninetransferase (ALT) 44 U/L
Creatinekinase 440 U/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 16 mm/h
What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: The two top differentials here that one should think about is polymyositis and polymyalgia rheumatica. Proximal muscle weakness and raised creatinine kinase points towards polymyositis.ESR is elevated in 50% of cases in polymyositis but correlates poorly with disease activity and response to therapy. In this stem, ESR is not elevated enough to consider polymyalgia rheumatica. Also, in polymyalgia rheumatica, creatinine kinase would not be raised. One of the criteria for the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica is having an ESR >30 mm/h or CRP >6 mg/mLof which we do not see in this stem. Hence, the best answer here is polymyositis. Polymyositis Clinical Findings First presents with difficulty with tasks that involve the proximal muscles:lifting objects, combing hair, getting up from the chair. The weakness is usually symmetric and diffuse, involving the proximal musclesof the neck, shoulders, trunk, hips, and thighs, the lower limb muscles tendingto be clinically symptomatic first. Fatigue, myalgia and muscle cramps may also be present. Investigation: Elevation of creatine kinase. Aldolase levels may also be raised. Autoantibodies: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies. Note that these are more common in patients with polymyositis than in patients with dermatomyositis. Muscle biopsy can be diagnostic. Treatment Involves steroids @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: DCIS (ductal carcinoma insitu) DCIS - high risk for progression to invasive ductal cancer Ducts are present in breast of males and females – hence ductal carcinoma is common in both males and females Lobules are seen in females only – hence lobular carcinoma is common in females exclusively. Classification of DCIS is based on Nuclear grade Necrosis Types of DCIS Low grade DCIS Cribriform Papillary Micropapillary High grade DCIS Solid Comedocarcinoma Investigations On mammography – presence of microcalcifications due to necrosis Most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of DCIS – MRI Most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of microcalcification in DCIS – mammography Treatment Non palpable DCIS – excision by needle localization with specimen mammography For low grade DCIS – Lumpectomy For DCIS with limited disease – Lumpectomy + RT @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
DCIS (ductal carcinoma insitu)

  • DCIS - high risk for progression to invasive ductal cancer
  • Ducts are present in breast of males and females – hence ductal carcinoma is common in both males and females
  • Lobules are seen in females only – hence lobular carcinoma is common in females exclusively.

Classification of DCIS is based on

  • Nuclear grade
  • Necrosis

Types of DCIS

Low grade DCIS

  • Cribriform
  • Papillary
  • Micropapillary

High grade DCIS

  • Solid
  • Comedocarcinoma

Investigations

  • On mammography – presence of microcalcifications due to necrosis
  • Most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of DCIS – MRI
  • Most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of microcalcification in DCIS – mammography

Treatment

  • Non palpable DCIS – excision by needle localization with specimen mammography
  • For low grade DCIS – Lumpectomy
  • For DCIS with limited disease – Lumpectomy + RT

Acute appendicitis

  • MC general surgical emergency worldwide

questions.solution: Generalised seizures usually have patients with a loss of consciousness (i.e. “collapsed”) while partial seizures may or may not have loss of consciousness depending if they are simple or complex. When both halves of the body (right and left) are involved, it is classified as generalised. In this case, this patient’s seizure activity is due to alcohol abuse and therefore should follow guidelines on management related to seizures secondary to alcoholism. Stiffness is the tonic phase followed by twitching which is the clonic phase. Myoclonic seizures are irregular jerks of the trunk or limbs which occur while the patient is conscious and lasts for less than a second. Most of us have this experience when we are falling asleep and suddenly jerk as if we fell down from a building. That is considered a normal phenomenon. Myoclonic seizures in an awake state are not normal and require specialist assessment. @Neet_pg_bot

Clinical features

  • Nonspecific respiratory symptoms including dyspnoea, chest pain andhaemoptysis. Bronchiectasis may progress to respiratory failure and corpulmonale - Coarse crackles are the most common finding, heard in early inspiration andoften in the lower zones
  • Large airway rhonchi (low-pitched snore-like sounds)
  • Wheeze may be present
  • Clubbing is found infrequently

Diagnosis

  • Usually made clinically, with high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) chestfor confirmation.
  • A baseline chest x-ray should be done in all patients. Early chest x-ray findingsmay be normal in patients with bronchiectasis. Chest x-ray in advanced casesmay show 1 to 2 cm cysts, crowding of the bronchi (tramlines) or ring opacities. The main value of CXR is excluding other causes of symptoms.
  • Rx
    • Antibiotic for 10–14 days.
      • NTM infection: Macrolide with rifampin and ethambutol
    • Hydration
    • Mucolytic: Dornase (DNase)→Only for CF-related bronchiectasis
    • Bronchodilator
    • Hypertonic saline
    • Chest physiotherapy
    • Pulmonary rehabilitation
    • Refractory cases:
      • Resection of a focal area
      • Lung transplantation.

questions.solution: A bone marrow biopsy with abundance of plasma cells is diagnostic for multiple myeloma. Multiple Myeloma Epidemiology: 50–60 years of age. Multiple myeloma is the most common tumor arising within the bone. Cytogenetic abnormalities: t(4;14) in which fibroblast growth factor receptor gene is translocated adjacent to the Ig heavy-chain gene; also, 13q deletions. Lytic lesions in the bone due to the expansion of plasma cells, which can predispose to pathologic fractures. Production of IL-6 by neoplastic cells stimulates osteoclasts through the RANK ligand. Hypercalcemia due to bone resorption. Decreased levels of functional immunoglobin predispose patients to recurrent infections (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Escherichia coli). Overproduction of the light chains, which collect in the kidney as casts in the distal convoluted tubules and collecting tubules. The light chains can cause renal insufficiency. Amyloidosis due to the overproduction of light chains. Important points regarding multiple myeloma Almost 99% of multiple myelomas secrete Ig. There is no M spike in nonsecretory myelomas. Approximately 60% of multiple myelomas produce IgG; 20–25% produce IgA; and 15–20% produce light chains only (κ or λ). The main cause of death is infection , and the second most common cause of death is renal failure. Approximately 20% of patients with multiple myeloma do not have a detectable M protein, but they do have free light chains in the urine. questions.solutionHtml:
A bone marrow biopsy with abundance of plasma cells is diagnostic for multiple myeloma.

Multiple Myeloma

Epidemiology:50–60 years of age. Multiple myeloma is the most common tumor arising within the bone.

Cytogenetic abnormalities: t(4;14) in which fibroblast growth factor receptor gene is translocated adjacent to the Ig heavy-chain gene; also, 13q deletions.

Clinical presentation of multiple myeloma

Symptoms:Bone pain, infection.

Signs:“Punched out” lesions of the skull seen on plain films are classic. Compression fractures of the vertebrae and pathologic fractures of the long bones are common, as is hypercalcemia.

Patients have renal failure associated with enlarged kidneys.

Complications of multiple myeloma

The most common bones involved are the vertebrae, skull, and ribs.

Bone pain due to expansion of marrow.

Lytic lesions in the bone due to the expansion of plasma cells, which can predispose to pathologic fractures. Production of IL-6 by neoplastic cells stimulates osteoclasts through the RANK ligand.

Hypercalcemia due to bone resorption.

Decreased levels of functional immunoglobin predispose patients to recurrent infections (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Escherichia coli).

Overproduction of the light chains, which collect in the kidney as casts in the distal convoluted tubules and collecting tubules. The light chains can cause renal insufficiency.

Amyloidosis due to the overproduction of light chains.

Important points regarding multiple myeloma

Almost 99% of multiple myelomas secrete Ig. There is no M spike in nonsecretory myelomas.

Approximately 60% of multiple myelomas produce IgG; 20–25% produce IgA; and 15–20% produce light chains only (κ or λ).

The main cause of death isinfection, and the second most common cause of death isrenal failure.

Approximately 20% of patients with multiple myeloma do not have a detectable M protein, but they do have free light chains in the urine.

Microscopic morphology of multiple myeloma (Figure 12-23 A and B)

More than 30% of bone marrow cells are plasma cells.

Accumulation of immunoglobins in plasma cells (Russell bodies).

questions.solutionHtml:
THORACIC OUTLET COMPRESSION SYNDROME

  • Characterized by compression of subclavian vessels and nerves of brachial plexus at thoracic inlet, therefore it is a misnomer
  • MC in middle age females
  • It is of 2 two types
    • Neurogenic form because of compression of brachial plexus
    • Vascular form →because of compression of subclavian vessels
  • Compression in TOS is
    • Dynamic
    • So, best diagnosed by provocative tests

Thoracic outlet space is created by

  1. Clavicle
  2. Firstrib
  3. Subclavius muscle
  4. Anterior scalene muscle
  5. Costoclavicular ligament

Predisposing factors for TOS

  1. Cervical rib / Abnormal first rib / fibrous band
  2. Long transverse process of
  3. Osteoarthritis
  4. Pancoast tumor Cervicalhaematoma

Clinical Manifestation

  • In Neurogenic form
    • MC involved route value MC involved nerve - Ulnar nerve
    • Patients complains of Pain, Paraesthesia along inner aspect of forearm andhand
    • On examination, Atrophy of hypothenar and interossei muscles is seen
  • On Arterial compression - has Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paralysis, Paraesthesia
  • In Venous form-has Pain, Cyanosis, Edema

Diagnosed by provocative test

  1. Adson's test (Scalene test)
  2. Costoclavicular Test (military position or Halsted test)
  3. Hyperabduction test (Wright test)
  4. Roos test (Arm claudication test)
  • Numbness ‡ pain ishands with exercise

Management

  • >90% patients are of Neurogenic form - Treated Conservatively
  • improvement in postural sitting, standing and sleeping positions
  • Advice Muscle stretching and strengthening exercise Indications of surgical intervention are

Indications of surgical intervention are

  1. Failure of conservative mx.
  2. Progression of sensory or motor symptoms.
  3. Excessively prolonged ulnar or median nerve conduction velocity
  4. Narrowing/ occlusion of subclavian artery
  5. Thrombosis of axillary/ subclavian vein
  6. Presence of anatomical abnormality

questions.solution: Placenta succenturiate One (usual) or more small lobes of placenta, size of a cotyledon, may be placed at varying distances from the main placental margin. A leash of vessels connecting the main to the small lobe traverse through the membranes. Upon inspection of the placenta after explusion, deficiency in the membranes on the periphery point to a succenturiate lobe. · Retention of a succenturiate lobe after pregnancy may lead to the following complications- (1) Postpartum hemorrhage which may be primary or secondary (2) Subinvolution (3) Uterine sepsis (4) Polyp formation. Treatment- When a succenturiate lobe is suspected, explore the uterus under general anaesthesia and remove the lobe. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Upon inspection of the placenta after explusion, deficiency in the membranes on the periphery point to a succenturiate lobe. ·
  • Retention of a succenturiate lobe after pregnancy may lead to the following complications- (1) Postpartum hemorrhage which may be primary or secondary (2) Subinvolution (3) Uterine sepsis (4) Polyp formation.
  • Treatment- When a succenturiate lobe is suspected, explore the uterus under general anaesthesia and remove the lobe.

questions.stemHtml: After tumbling down the stairs and breaking her rib, a 38-year-old lady is sent to A&E. Shortness of breath is a complaint she has. To rule out a rib fracture, a chest X-ray was taken. The chest X-ray revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. There are vesicular breath sounds on auscultation. questions.solution: whenever you see the term “bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy” with a lesion on the shin, you should be thinking of Sarcoidosis. The lesion on the shin is erythema nodosum which are blue or red lesions and are seen in people suffering from sarcoidosis. The syndrome here is Lofgren syndrome which includes erythema nodosum, arthritis, and hilar adenopathy. Lofgren is a distinct sarcoid syndrome. SARCODIOSIS Sarcoidosis is a systemic disease of unknown cause, characterized histologically by the presence of nonspecific noncaseatinggranulomas in the lung and other organs. Presentation Up to 50% are asymptomatic (Chest X-ray for another indication reveals the diagnosis from hilar lymphadenopathy) Involves almost any organ system, but pulmonary involvement is most common (around 90% of symptomatic patients) Fatigue Skin: Erythema nodosum Lymphadenopathy Eyes: Uveitis Kidneys: Stones Acute presentation usually have the following: Erythema nodosum Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy Fever Polyathralgia There are two distinct sarcoid syndromes with acute presentation Lofgren syndrome includes: Erythema nodosum Arthritis Hilar adenopathy Heerfordt-Waldenstrom syndrome, which described Fever Parotid enlargement Uveitis Facial palsy Investigations Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilaradenopathy Bloods: Elevation in angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) can be seen in of patients with sarcoidosis (but remember that ACE should not be used diagnose sarcoidosis. ACE levels are nonspecific but can be used to follow the course of the disease.) Abnormalities in liver function tests are seen in of patients Pulmonary function test may show a restrictive pattern Calcium levels (Hypercalcaemia can occur due to increased circulation of vitamin D produced by macrophages) Definitive diagnosis is by biopsy of suspected tissue which shows noncaseating granulomas. This can be from skin, lymph nodes, conjunctiva or lung. @Neet_pg_bot

Sarcoidosis is a systemic disease of unknown cause, characterized histologically by the presence of nonspecific noncaseatinggranulomas in the lung and other organs.

Presentation

  • Up to 50% are asymptomatic (Chest X-ray for another indication reveals the diagnosis from hilar lymphadenopathy)
  • Involves almost any organ system, but pulmonary involvement is most common (around 90% of symptomatic patients)
  • Fatigue
  • Skin: Erythema nodosum
  • Lymphadenopathy
  • Eyes: Uveitis
  • Kidneys: Stones

Acute presentation usually have the following:

  • Erythema nodosum
  • Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
  • Fever
  • Polyathralgia

There are two distinct sarcoid syndromes with acute presentation

  • Lofgren syndrome includes:
    • Erythema nodosum
    • Arthritis
    • Hilar adenopathy
  • Heerfordt-Waldenstrom syndrome, which described
    • Fever
    • Parotid enlargement
    • Uveitis
    • Facial palsy

Investigations

  • Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilaradenopathy
  • Bloods:
    • Elevation in angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) can be seen in of patients with sarcoidosis (but remember that ACE should not be used diagnose sarcoidosis. ACE levels are nonspecific but can be used to follow the course of the disease.)
    • Abnormalities in liver function tests are seen in of patients
    • Pulmonary function test may show a restrictive pattern
    • Calcium levels (Hypercalcaemia can occur due to increased circulation of vitamin D produced by macrophages)
  • Definitive diagnosis is by biopsy of suspected tissue which shows noncaseating granulomas. This can be from skin, lymph nodes, conjunctiva or lung.

questions.solutionHtml:
The collapse could be due to hypoglycaemia. Check venous or capillary blood with glucose oxidase strip would be an appropriate first step before taking him for a CT scan or any other investigation. It is fast, easy and if hypoglycaemia is the cause, it can be quickly reversible.

Hyopglycaemia

Always exclude hypoglycaemia in any patient with coma, altered behaviour, neurological symptoms, or signs

Causes

  • Commonest cause is a relative imbalance of administered versus required insulin or oral hypoglycaemic drug. This results from
    • Exercise
    • Insufficient or delayed food intake
    • Excessive insulin administration

Other causes are:

  • Alcohol (in addition to alcohol directly causing hypoglycaemia, the features of hypoglycaemia may be mistaken for alcohol intoxication or withdrawal)
  • Addison’s disease
  • Insulinomas
  • Liver failure
  • Malaria

Common features:

Plasma glucose is normally maintained at 3.6-5.8mmol/L. Cognitive function deteriorates at levels<3.0mmol/L, but symptoms are uncommon >2.5mmol/L

  • Sweating
  • Pallor
  • Tachycarida
  • Palpitations
  • Hunger
  • Trembling
  • Altered or loss consciousness
  • Fitting
  • Coma

Diagnosis

  • Venous or capillary blood with glucose oxidase strip (BMG)
  • If <3.0 mmol/L, take a venous sample for a formal blood glucose level, but do not delay treatment

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency with severe back pain that radiates down his legs, as well as urine retention and incontinence. Perineal sensory loss is discovered during the examination. What is the ONE inquiry that is the MOST APPROPRIATE?
questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency with severe back pain that radiates down his legs, as well as urine retention and incontinence. Perineal sensory loss is discovered during the examination. What is the ONE inquiry that is the MOST APPROPRIATE?
questions.solution: This is a classic example of cauda equina syndrome. It is a serious neurologic condition in which damage to the cauda equina causes loss of function of the nerve roots of the spinal canal below the termination (conus medullaris) of the spinal cord. Any lesion which compresses or disturbs the function of the cauda equina may disable the nerves although the most common is a central disc prolapse. Investigation of choice is an MRI. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: All of the following are true regarding retrocochlear sensorineural hearing loss except:
questions.stemHtml: All of the following are true regarding retrocochlear sensorineural hearing loss except:
questions.solution: Recruitment is a phenomenon of abnormal growth of loudness. The ear which does not hear low intensity sound begins to hear greater intensity sounds as loud or even louder than normal hearing ear. Thus, a loud sound which is tolerable in normal ear may grow to abnormal levels of loudness in the recruiting ear and thus becomes intolerable. The patients with recruitment are poor candidates for hearing aids. Recruitment is typically seen in lesions of the cochlea (e.g. Meniere's disease and presbycusis) and thus helps to differentiate a cochlear from a retrocochlear sensorineural hearing loss. @Neet_pg_bot
